papers.title: MidasTUI: Instant Tangible User Interfaces for Wearable Displays using Everyday Objects
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34945v1

summary.one_liner: MidasTUI turns ordinary objects into temporary input devices for wearable displays by using the headset camera and a Transformer-based temporal classifier to detect hand-object motion, infer the intended input type (slider, mouse, keypad), and map it to an app function.
summary.plain: Wearable displays such as smart glasses can show a full workspace, but controlling them usually means waving your hands in the air, which is tiring and gives no physical feedback, or carrying a separate controller. This paper proposes using everyday objects instead: for example, sliding an earbud case across a table can act as a mouse. The system watches the user's hand through the display's camera, works out what kind of control the motion is meant to be, and links it to an action on screen.
summary.why:
The work addresses a practical usability problem for head-worn displays, and it reports a comparative user study claiming lower physical burden and better perceived usability than mid-air gestures. The text gives no detailed numbers, so the strength of these claims can't be judged from this summary alone; it may matter for how future wearable interfaces handle input.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Tangible user interface: a control built from physical objects a person can touch, rather than purely on-screen or in-air controls.
- Wearable display: a head-worn screen (such as smart glasses) that overlays digital content on the real world.
- Mid-air gestures: hand movements made without touching anything, which can cause arm fatigue and offer no tactile feedback.
- Temporal classifier: a machine-learning model that labels sequences of sensor data over time; a Transformer is a common neural-network architecture for this.
- Cross-object and cross-user generalization: whether the system still works on objects and people it was not trained on.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">intermediate

papers.abstract: While wearable displays can bring digital workspaces anywhere, interaction remains limited by mid-air gestures that lack tactile feedback and induce fatigue, or controllers that are cumbersome to carry. We present MidasTUI, a system that instantly transforms arbitrary everyday objects into opportunistic tangible user interfaces through brief interaction demonstrations. For example, a user can slide an earbud case across a table as a mouse, enabling opportunistic interaction without carrying a dedicated input device. MidasTUI detects when a user is holding and moving an object using the wearable display camera and a Transformer-based temporal classifier. It then infers the intended input modality (e.g., slider, mouse, keypad) from hand movement and maps the tracked hand-object interaction to an application function. Our evaluations demonstrate reliable cross-object and cross-user generalization. A comparative user study further shows that grounding interaction in everyday objects reduces physical burden and improves perceived usability and control relative to mid-air interaction.

papers.title: Towards Democratized Academic LLM Hosting: Practical insights from needs, implementations, and governance across Dutch institutions
authors: the Towards Democratized Academic LLM Hosting Workshop Consortium
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34383v1

summary.background:
- LLM (large language model): the kind of AI behind chatbots and text-generating tools.
- Hosting: running the software on one's own servers or a managed environment, rather than only using a company's website or API.
- Institutionally governed: the university sets the rules on access, data, and responsible use.
- Democratized access: making such tools available broadly across an institution, not just to well-funded groups.
- Socio-technical: involving both technology and the people, rules, and organizations around it.
- Energy and utilization: how much electricity the hardware uses and how much of its capacity is actually used.
- Dutch academia: the universities and research institutes in the Netherlands.
summary.one_liner: A workshop-based synthesis of needs, implementation practices, and governance challenges for institutionally hosted large language model (LLM) services across Dutch academic institutions.
summary.plain: Universities increasingly want to run their own AI chatbot-style tools instead of relying only on outside commercial services. This paper reports on a workshop with people from university IT, research support, education, and policy, and summarizes the practices, tensions, and open questions they raised. The text itself is a high-level overview; it does not report measured results.
summary.why: Decisions about where and how universities host AI tools touch on cost, energy use, data control, and fairness of access, so practical accounts of these choices are useful to people running or funding such services. The text is a short abstract-level description, so it is hard to judge how deep the findings go; it may be most relevant to research-infrastructure and digital-policy readers.

papers.abstract: Academic LLM hosting is emerging as an operational infrastructure domain with recurring socio-technical patterns, tensions, and governance requirements across institutions. Based on a workshop with academic infrastructure, research-support, education, and policy-adjacent stakeholders, this paper synthesizes current practices and open questions around institutionally governed LLM services for Dutch academia. It highlights challenges around deployment models, energy and utilization, governance, tooling, commercial integration, and research and education use cases, and identifies emerging directions for service pathways, coordination, and responsible operation.

papers.title: Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32768v1

summary.background:
- A "model spec" is a written document from an AI developer describing the intended behaviour of its AI model, including what it should and should not do.
- "Frontier AI developers" means the organisations building the most capable, cutting-edge AI models.
- A "taxonomy" is a structured classification of types or categories, here of model specs.
- "Governance" refers to the rules, oversight and institutions that guide how a technology is developed and used.
- Model specs are a fairly new kind of document, so there is no settled standard for them yet.
summary.one_liner: This paper offers a five-part guide to writing "model specs" (public documents stating how frontier AI models should behave), covering benefits, a taxonomy, practical writing and implementation guidance, eight open problems, and recommendations for companies, governments and civil society.
summary.plain: AI companies are starting to publish documents that describe how their AI systems are meant to behave, and there has been little independent advice on how to write them. This paper tries to fill that gap by explaining why such documents help, sorting them into a rough classification, suggesting how to write and apply them, and listing unresolved questions. The text provided is a summary of the paper's structure; it does not show the specific content of the guidance or the taxonomy.
summary.why: As AI systems become more influential, publicly stated behaviour rules are becoming part of how these systems are developed and governed, so practical guidance on them may matter to developers, regulators and the public. The text does not show how widely the proposals have been adopted or tested, so their real impact is unclear.

papers.abstract: Frontier AI developers from around the world have begun to publish documents that describe how their AI models are intended to behave. Although these 'model specifications'-or 'model specs', for short-are increasingly important in AI development and governance, little independent guidance exists for writing them. This paper addresses this gap in five main sections. First, we outline the advantages of writing a model spec for AI developers and society at large. Second, we introduce a taxonomy for model specs that developers can take inspiration from. Third, we propose guidance for writing and implementing a spec in practice. Fourth, we note eight open problems related to writing model specs for safe and desirable behaviour. We conclude with recommendations for frontier AI companies, governments, and research and civil society organisations.

papers.title: Calm Agent: Reframing Agent Interaction around Intermittent Human Attention
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32009v1

summary.background:
- AI agent: software that carries out multi-step tasks on a user's behalf with some autonomy.
- Intermittent attention: a person who looks at a task only occasionally while doing other work.
- Persistent task representation: a continuing internal record of what a task is, its status, and its settings, so users can pick it up again.
- Generative interaction: interfaces an AI creates on the fly to fit an open-ended goal, versus fixed, pre-built controls.
- Human-computer interaction (HCI): the field studying how people use and design computer systems.
- Position paper: a text that argues for a viewpoint and proposes a framework, typically without a full empirical evaluation.
summary.one_liner: This position paper proposes "Calm Agent," a design framework for AI agents running ongoing background tasks that organizes three on-demand interaction modes (Delegate, Adjust, Check) around a persistent task representation, and illustrates it with a desktop prototype called Orvlet.
summary.plain: The paper argues that AI helpers doing side tasks should be designed for people who only check in now and then, because their attention is elsewhere. The authors describe a way to structure this: users hand off a task, tune it, or glance at its status, with the task's state kept in one continuing record. They show the ideas through a desktop prototype, Orvlet, but the text does not report user testing or measured results.
summary.why: As AI agents start running tasks for long stretches in the background, how people keep track of and steer them without being pulled away from their main work is an open design question. The paper's framing may be relevant to interface design and attention research, though its evidence is a position and prototype description rather than a study.

papers.abstract: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention: tasks should continue between interactions, and users should be able to return with little effort to understand and control them. We develop this position as Calm Agent. It connects three on-demand interaction modes: Delegate, Adjust, and Check, through a persistent task representation. Generative interaction provides controls and feedback suited to open-ended goals, while existing controls support routine actions. We illustrate these principles with Orvlet, a desktop prototype for background execution and compact task interfaces. We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.

papers.title: Neurosymbolic Human-AI Collaboration: Foundations, Conceptual Framework, and Applications
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28011v1

summary.background:
- Human-AI collaboration (HAIC): people and AI sharing a task, each covering the other's weaknesses.
- Machine learning: software that learns patterns from data, such as recognizing images or speech.
- Explainable AI: methods that try to make a model's reasoning understandable to people.
- Neurosymbolic AI: combining neural networks (pattern learning from data) with symbolic reasoning (explicit rules and concepts).
- Semantic gap: the mismatch between how a machine represents information and how humans think about it.
- Human-in-the-loop vs. human-on-the-loop: a person actively approves each AI decision versus a person supervising and intervening when needed.
summary.one_liner: This paper proposes NeSy-HAIC, a conceptual framework that uses neurosymbolic AI (combining neural networks with symbolic reasoning) to give humans and AI a shared, human-readable interface for collaborating on tasks, illustrated with semi-autonomous driving and security alert prioritization.
summary.plain: Many workplaces now have people and AI systems working on the same tasks, but it is still hard for them to understand each other. This paper proposes a conceptual blueprint, called NeSy-HAIC, that mixes two styles of AI so the machine's internal workings can be expressed as concepts people already understand. The authors sketch how this could work in two example settings, self-driving cars that still need a human driver and ranking security alerts, but the text describes the framework rather than reporting tested results.
summary.why: Getting humans and AI to communicate clearly is a long-standing obstacle in human-AI collaboration, and the paper ties that problem to explainable AI and neurosymbolic methods. Because it is a framework proposal without reported experiments in the text, its practical value is still to be shown.

papers.abstract: The growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across workplaces and industries, ranging from manufacturing plants to healthcare facilities, has paved the way to the design of systems in which humans and AI collaborate on shared tasks. The first developments of Human-AI Collaboration (HAIC) were driven by advances in Machine Learning (ML), which enabled the automation of numerous tasks, including large-scale data processing, image analysis, and speech recognition. However, ML automation have proven insufficient for certain applications due to methodological, safety, and ethical concerns. In such cases, researchers argue for integrating human expertise into operational workflows to improve performance, relying on the complementary skill sets of humans and AI. Despite long-standing research, the field of HAIC has not yet reached full maturity, largely due to the intrinsic difficulty of ensuring a seamless communication between humans and AI. This challenge is partially addressed by Explainable AI methods, which aim to make internal model reasoning more transparent through human-understandable explanations. Recognizing the need for a shared interface between humans and AI in collaborative settings, we propose a novel conceptual framework, NeSy-HAIC, that leverages Neurosymbolic AI (NeSy AI) to bridge the semantic gap between machine representations and human-understandable symbolic concepts. The framework builds on current research in NeSy AI and HAIC, supports multiple interaction paradigms, including Human-In-The-Loop and Human-On-The-Loop, and is characterized through its enabling methodologies and two illustrative use cases in semi-autonomous driving and security alert prioritization. We argue that the integration of data-driven learning and symbolic reasoning can substantially enhance human-AI interaction and mitigate limitations of collaborative systems.

papers.title: Pharmacy stock and post-earthquake access to medicines in Tokyo: modeling choices that change recovery judgments
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29459v1

summary.background:
- Accessibility model: estimates how easily people can reach a service on foot, based on distance and how many providers are nearby.
- Floating catchment area method: a common accessibility calculation that assigns each location a supply-to-demand ratio using nearby providers and people; the paper compares four variants.
- Retention: post-disaster accessibility divided by the same location's pre-disaster accessibility (1 means no loss).
- Stock depletion: pharmacies run out of medicine over time, so their capacity to serve people falls even if the building is open.
- Scenario earthquake: a hypothetical event used for planning and simulation, not a real event.
- Rank correlation and Jaccard index: measures of how similar two rankings are overall, and how much two sets of "lowest 10%" areas overlap (0.56 means partial overlap).
- Percentile: the 10th-percentile result is a low-end outcome, worse than most sampled cases.
summary.one_liner: A sensitivity study of a two-step floating catchment accessibility model for over-the-counter medicine access at Tokyo pharmacies after a scenario magnitude-7.3 earthquake, showing that stock-depletion assumptions, model type and floating-catchment method choices can change recovery verdicts.
summary.plain: After a major earthquake, people need nearby pharmacies to still be open, staffed and holding medicine. This paper simulates over-the-counter medicines at about 4,700 registered pharmacies in Tokyo's 23 wards during the first week after a scenario quake, and measures how walking access compares with pre-quake levels. The authors find that the answer to "is access recovering?" depends heavily on how one models pharmacies running low on stock, on the kind of model used, and on which method is chosen.
summary.why: Local decisions about where to prioritise pharmacy support may hinge on modelling choices that are rarely reported, so the paper argues for stating stock assumptions and worst-case (low-end) outcomes. The relevance beyond Tokyo is plausible but the text covers only one city and one scenario.

papers.abstract: Community pharmacies sustain access to medicines after an earthquake only while open, staffed and stocked. Accessibility models rarely represent stock depletion, and the assumptions this requires may change conclusions about recovery. We examine these assumptions for over-the-counter (OTC) medicines supplied by 4,748 registered pharmacies in Tokyo's 23 wards during the first week after a magnitude-7.3 scenario earthquake. A two-step floating catchment area model computes walking accessibility for 2,651 grid cells (500 m) under 10,000 sampled combinations of stock duration, staffing, operation and demand. Results are expressed as Retention: post-disaster accessibility divided by the same cell's pre-disaster accessibility. First, the assumed link between stock and service, the supply a pharmacy can still provide, determines the recovery verdict. If service falls in proportion to remaining stock, mean Retention declines from 0.479 (days 2-3) to 0.273 (days 4-7). If service is maintained until stock falls below one quarter, the mean rises instead, although low-end (10th-percentile) outcomes still decline. Measuring at the start of each period rather than averaging over it also reverses the trend. Second, a simple model that rescales a fixed map by citywide supply and demand reproduces citywide patterns but cannot evaluate where pharmacies close or where capacity is added; a spatial model run once on average inputs can. Third, four floating catchment methods agree on overall rankings (rank correlation 0.81), but their lowest-ranked 10% of cells overlap only partially (Jaccard index 0.56). Disaster assessments should report stock assumptions and low-end outcomes, and treat local priority areas as method-dependent.

papers.title: AROMA: Understanding AI Support For Mental Well-being through Role Theory
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26843v1

summary.background:
- Role theory: a social-science idea that people behave according to expected parts in a relationship, such as counselor or friend.
- Relational harm: damage to trust or the relationship when one party behaves in unexpected ways.
- Annotation: human labeling of data (here, conversation turns) to create a coded dataset.
- Role States: the paper's term for eight behavior categories inferred from what speakers actually did, not from what they were told to do.
- Prompting strategy: instructions written to steer a language model's behavior.
- Structural and temporal characteristics: how conversation turns are organized and how roles shift over the course of a conversation.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes AROMA, a role-oriented framework that annotates over 7,515 conversations from 13 datasets to derive eight observed "Role States" for AI mental well-being supporters, and uses them to analyze support contexts, structural and temporal differences from humans, and a prompting strategy for better role alignment.
summary.plain: AI chatbots that offer emotional support sometimes act outside the role they were meant to play, and this can hurt the relationship with the user. Standard tests only check whether such bots work in narrow tasks, so they miss why these mismatches happen. The authors labeled thousands of real conversations from 13 datasets by the roles the speakers actually took, and identified eight recurring role patterns.
summary.why: The work offers a shared vocabulary for describing when and how AI supporters drift from their intended role, which may help explain failures that task-based evaluations overlook. The text does not report how much the proposed prompting strategy improves outcomes, so its practical impact is unclear from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: AI supporters for mental well-being are becoming more prevalent. When these AI supporters start acting in ways beyond their expected function it leads to relational harm. Standard approaches to evaluating such AI supporters are limited to inspecting their efficacy in narrow task-specific settings, which do not explain these discrepancies in expected and actual behavior. To address this gap, we propose the AROMA (A Role-Oriented Model of Analysis) framework to provide a common role taxonomy for different support contexts. We developed AROMA using a theory-informed annotation of over 7,515 conversations from 13 datasets and propose eight "Role States" based on observed-not prescribed-behavior. We show these Role States vary according to the context of support; depict unique structural and temporal characteristics of AI supporters vis-a-vis Humans; and inform novel AI support prompting strategy for better role alignment. This framework provides a new lens to understand AI support failures.

papers.title: A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27189v1

summary.background:
- Foundation model: a very large AI model trained on huge datasets, costly in computing power and money.
- Compute: the processing power (and electricity) needed to train or run AI.
- Responsible AI: designing AI to be fair, safe, transparent and accountable.
- Digital public infrastructure: shared government-built digital systems (such as identity or payment platforms) that others can build on.
- Sovereignty: a country's ability to control, inspect and adapt the technology it relies on.
- Vernacular-first: designing for local languages before English.
- Right-sized model: the smallest model that meets a defined requirement with a safety margin.
summary.one_liner: A CeRAI (IIT Madras) white paper proposing "Responsible Frugal AI" as a right-sized, resource-conscious policy and engineering framework for deploying AI at population scale in India, with seven levers, a seven-point checklist and eleven policy statements.
summary.plain: This white paper argues that India should not try to copy the huge, expensive AI models built in the US or China, nor simply use foreign AI with local tweaks. Instead it proposes a third approach: use the smallest AI system that does the job well enough, with careful checks, human oversight for serious decisions, and limits on total resource use. The authors frame this as a policy and design guide rather than a set of experimental results.
summary.why: India must serve a very large and varied population under tight budgets and uneven infrastructure, so a cost-aware approach to AI is a practical question for public services. The text is a position paper with a framework and checklist; it does not report measured outcomes, so its practical effect is untested from this text alone.

papers.abstract: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. This white paper from the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras, proposes a third path: Responsible Frugal AI, which applies principle-based frugal engineering alongside Responsible AI. Responsible Frugal AI is right-sized AI: it fixes the functional requirement first, asks whether AI is needed at all, and then chooses the smallest sufficient model, meeting the requirement with minimal resources while keeping a verified margin, robustness and responsible governance. The framework applies frugality across four dimensions (data, compute, model and operations) through seven levers spanning the AI lifecycle, each with practices and measures. It calls for public AI rails, vernacular-first design, measured resource use, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, and a cap on total resource consumption so that efficiency gains are not cancelled out by rising usage. We argue that India is resource-imbalanced rather than resource-poor, and that frugal principles offer the most viable route to population-scale deployment, fit naturally with India's digital public infrastructure, and make sovereignty operational by preserving India's capacity to specify, deploy, govern, inspect and adapt its AI systems. A seven-point adoption checklist and eleven policy statements translate the framework into practice, positioning AI in India as a responsible, frugal public-value system that maximises social value per rupee and per joule.

papers.title: Rethinking Utility in Differentially Private Visualization: A Channel-Centric Perspective
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26396v1

summary.background:
- Differential privacy (DP): a method that adds carefully calibrated random noise to data or results so that no single person's record can be identified, at a cost to accuracy.
- Visualization: turning data into charts or graphics for people to read.
- Visual channels: the visual properties that carry data values, such as position, length, angle, area, or color.
- Utility: how useful or accurate a privatized output remains for the reader's task.
- Perceptual effectiveness: how reliably people read a given visual property accurately.
- Channel-read-mechanism hypothesis (from the paper): the idea that usefulness depends jointly on which reading a chart makes easy and on which DP mechanism adds the noise.
summary.one_liner: A position-style synthesis that reframes prior findings on differentially private (DP) visualization through the lens of visual channels (position, color, size, etc.), proposing a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis and identifying gaps in evaluation research.
summary.plain: Protecting private data often means adding random noise to it before it is charted, and that noise can make charts harder to read. This paper looks across earlier studies of how this noise affects different charts and argues that the way information is visually encoded, such as by position, length, or color, matters as much as the privacy method used. It proposes a working hypothesis for this and points to gaps in how these charts are currently tested.
summary.why: As more organizations publish charts built from sensitive data, knowing which visual designs stay readable under privacy noise helps both designers and privacy engineers. The text is a synthesis and hypothesis rather than a set of new experiments, so its claims are proposals to be tested, not established results.

papers.abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to protect sensitive data in visualization, but understanding how privacy-induced noise affects visual representations remains fragmented. Prior work has examined the impact of DP noise on specific chart types, yet these findings are typically tied to particular chart types and evaluation settings, making it difficult to generalize across contexts. In parallel, visualization research has long established that visual channels, the visual properties of marks that encode data attributes, differ in perceptual effectiveness under noise-free conditions. However, these principles have not been systematically revisited under DP, where noise is deliberately introduced into the data to protect privacy. In this paper, we present a channel-centric perspective to reframe prior empirical and theoretical results. Our synthesis drawson prior findings to motivate a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis: the utility of DP visualizations may depend on the task-relevant reads made salient by visual channel configurations and DP mechanism choice jointly. Moreover, this perspective highlights the role of channel choice throughout the privacy-preserving visualization pipeline, from disclosure framing and DP algorithm design to utility evaluation and interpretation of noisy outputs. The synthesis also identifies gaps in the existing evaluation literature and highlights research opportunities for channel-aware DP visualization.

papers.title: VideoTrail: Interactive Video Foraging Through Hierarchical Visualization
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25377v1

summary.background:
- Information foraging theory: a model from HCI that treats information seeking like animals hunting for food, following "scent" (cues that suggest where useful content lies).
- Scrubbing: dragging the playback bar to skip around a video.
- Hierarchical visualization: showing content at multiple levels of detail, such as broad sections that break down into smaller segments.
- Multimodal: using more than one kind of signal, here visual and text content.
- User study: an experiment where people perform tasks with a system, compared against a baseline; N=16 means 16 participants, a small sample.
summary.one_liner: VideoTrail is a browser extension that uses a hierarchical, multimodal visualization, framed through information foraging theory, to help users navigate and locate information in videos, evaluated in a 16-person user study against standard timelines.
summary.plain: People often watch videos to find a specific piece of information, but scrubbing through a progress bar is slow and hit-or-miss. This paper presents VideoTrail, a browser add-on that builds a map of a video's sections, with labels and structural cues, so viewers can jump toward the parts most likely to matter. In a study with 16 participants, the authors report that it helped them find key moments more efficiently than a traditional timeline and supported new ways of navigating.
summary.why: Video is a common but hard-to-search medium, and better navigation tools matter for learning, research, and everyday viewing. The work is a small-sample user study, so its findings are preliminary, but it connects human-computer interaction design with ideas about how people forage for information.

papers.abstract: People often watch videos to find information, but locating relevant moments can be difficult and time-consuming. Existing strategies like scrubbing rely primarily on visual scanning and linear search, providing limited support for goal-directed navigation. We present VideoTrail, an AI-powered browser extension that supports information seeking in videos through a hierarchical visualization. Inspired by information foraging theory, VideoTrail surfaces semantic and structural cues as information scent, creating an explorable roadmap of segments. The system is multimodal and adaptive, prioritizing visual or textual scent based on the video's content. In a user study (N=16), VideoTrail helped participants efficiently locate key moments and enabled new navigation strategies compared to traditional timelines, highlighting how exposing an adaptive video structure can enhance goal-directed viewing.

papers.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25263v1

summary.background:
- Deactivation experiment: participants are asked to stop using a tool for a set period, and outcomes are compared with a group that stops for less time (here, one day).
- Longitudinal: measurements taken over time, here including a follow-up two weeks after people resumed AI use.
- Loneliness and social interaction are measured through self-report and participants' descriptions of their time, as described in the text.
- β (beta) is a regression coefficient: the estimated size and direction of the effect. p-values indicate how likely a result this large would be by chance under the study's assumptions.
- Instrumental use means using a tool to get a practical job done, such as writing, planning, or research, as opposed to social or emotional use.
- Open-ended responses are free-text answers, used here to describe what people did instead of using AI, such as asking other people for help.
summary.one_liner: A randomized longitudinal deactivation experiment (N=625 active ChatGPT users) finds that a two-week break from general-purpose AI assistants, mostly used for instrumental tasks, reduced self-reported loneliness and increased in-person social interaction relative to a one-day control.
summary.plain: Many people now use AI chatbots like ChatGPT mainly for everyday work tasks rather than for companionship. This study asked whether giving those tools up for two weeks changes how lonely people feel and how much they socialize. Participants were randomly assigned to go without AI for either two weeks or one day, and the two-week group reported less loneliness and more in-person contact.
summary.why: Most research on AI and social life has looked at people using AI explicitly as companions, so this suggests that ordinary productivity use may also matter for connection. It is a single study as described in this text, and the authors' interpretation that AI may "inadvertently" reduce social contact is one reading of the data rather than a settled finding.

papers.abstract: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

papers.title: Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23825v1

summary.background:
- Character animation: making virtual figures move; games often use pre-recorded clips and state machines (rules for switching between clips).
- Motion capture: recording a real person's movements with sensors or cameras to use as reference data.
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training a program by rewarding behavior that achieves a goal; here a simulated character learns to move.
- Adversarial style rewards: a learned judge that rewards movements looking like the captured human motion.
- Task-specific rewards: extra scoring for goals such as hitting a target or evading an attack.
- Meta Quest: a consumer VR headset; the prototype runs on it.
- Tang Soo Do: a Korean martial art whose techniques informed the dataset.
summary.one_liner: A reinforcement-learning framework that pretrains a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from motion-capture data and adapts them with task rewards to animate VR sparring opponents, evaluated by a user study and a Meta Quest prototype.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to make computer-controlled fighters in virtual reality move like real martial artists, instead of relying only on hand-made animation clips. The authors recorded motion-capture data of Tang Soo Do techniques, learned a set of reusable movement skills from it, and then tuned those skills so the character can aim strikes at a target and dodge threats. Participants rated the resulting motions, and the team built a small VR sparring demo.
summary.why: Game opponents that move more varied and believable could reduce the labor of hand-authoring animations and make VR training or sparring feel more natural. The text reports a user study and a working prototype, but it does not give the study's results or sample size, so how strong the gains are cannot be judged from this text alone.

papers.abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.

papers.title: AI Companions for Young Adult Caregivers: Practical Advice, Emotional Depth, and the Limits of Metric Evaluation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23147v1

summary.background:
- Young adult caregivers (YACs): people aged 18 to 25 looking after a chronically ill person.
- Large language model (LLM): an AI system that generates text, here built on Gemma 3-27B, an openly released model.
- Fine-tuning: further training a model on a specific dataset so it behaves in a targeted way.
- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): the model looks up reference material before answering.
- LLM judge: another AI model used to automatically compare and score responses.
- Metric evaluation vs. user perception: automated scores versus what real people actually experience.
- Well-being experts: the paper's human reviewers who first chose the fine-tuned version.
summary.one_liner: This paper presents Carebot, a fine-tuned open-weight language model (Gemma 3-27B) for young adult caregivers aged 18 to 25, and reports a 90-participant user study showing that automated judge scores and user perceptions of its emotional versus practical tone diverged.
summary.plain: Many people aged 18 to 25 look after a sick family member, partner, or friend, and this paper asks whether an AI chat companion can help them. The authors built a version of an AI model tuned on conversations with these caregivers and a psychologist. Experts and an automated judge preferred it, but when 90 real caregivers tried it, they found it too practical and short on emotional support.
summary.why: It shows that a tool that scores well on automated tests can still feel wrong to the people it is meant to help, which matters for anyone evaluating AI support tools. The text does not show how well the findings would generalize beyond this one group and setup.

papers.abstract: Young adult caregivers (YACs) are individuals aged 18 to 25 currently taking care of a family member, partner, or friend facing chronic illness. AI companions designed specifically for YACs remain underexplored in prior works. We present Carebot, it uses an open-weight LLM (Gemma 3-27B) as its base model, on which we compared fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of both. The fine-tuning was performed based on an existing dataset of conversations with YACs and a psychologist. Three well-being experts evaluated these configurations and preferred the fine-tuned model for the warmth of its responses and its actionable advice tailored to YACs. Based on their choice, we adopted the fine-tuned model as Carebot's final configuration and used it for all subsequent evaluations. An LLM judge preferred this Carebot's responses over the base model's in 85% of evaluated pairs. We then conducted a user study with 90 YACs, half of whom interacted with the base model and half with Carebot. The user study revealed a discrepancy between metric evaluation and actual user perception. Participants who used Carebot were more likely to characterize its replies as overly practical and brief, noting that it favored advice over emotional support. Conversely, participants who used the base model indicated that its responses were more emotionally oriented than practical. Although, fine-tuning made Carebot's replies more practical, but they were not emotionally supportive for users. We argue that support tools for YACs require situation-sensitive emotional depth and aligned evaluation frameworks to study their effectiveness.

papers.title: The Whole Warps the Parts: Attentional Certainty Modulates Ensemble-Induced Bias in Visualizations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22885v1

summary.background:
- Ensemble statistics: summary properties (such as average size) computed across a set of similar objects.
- Ensemble-induced bias: an individual item's perceived value being shifted toward or away from the group average.
- Repulsion vs. attraction: repulsion means the item is judged further from the average; attraction means it is judged closer to it.
- Identification vs. discrimination: identification asks for the item's size directly; discrimination asks which of two sizes is larger.
- Pre-cue / post-cue / no-cue: whether the viewer is told which item to judge before or after seeing the group, or not told at all.
- Attentional certainty: how sure the viewer is about where to direct attention.
- Study 2 uses charts of startup valuations and precinct vote contributions as applied examples.
summary.one_liner: A visualization-perception study showing that whether a viewer knows in advance which item to judge within an ensemble of marks flips the direction of ensemble-induced bias from repulsion to attraction, with identification precision falling as target cues are removed.
summary.plain: When people look at a crowd of similar shapes, such as a group of circles on a chart, the overall average size of the group can pull their judgment of one circle away from or toward that average. This paper asks why earlier studies found opposite effects, and reports that the answer seems to be how certain the viewer is about which item to attend to. When the target circle was named beforehand, the group tended to push judgments away from the average; when no target was specified, the bias reversed and pulled judgments toward it.
summary.why: Charts and dashboards routinely ask people to read both group summaries and single values, so knowing when context distorts individual readings matters for design. The authors also extend the idea from precision alone to how attention-directing choices set which bias a viewer is subject to; the text does not show how far this generalizes beyond the tested displays.

papers.abstract: Data visualizations often require viewers to extract both ensemble statistics and individual values from collections of graphical marks. Yet individual items embedded within an ensemble can be systematically biased by that context. Prior studies have reported both repulsion away from and attraction toward ensemble statistics, but these effects have been observed across different conditions. We test whether task or attentional certainty explains these opposing forms of ensemble-induced bias. In Study 1, observers briefly viewed ensembles of differently sized circles and then judged the size of an individual circle embedded within the ensemble. Using a common stimulus generation framework, we tested both identification and discrimination when the target was specified before or after the ensemble, and an additional no-cue identification condition without a specified target. Under the shared cued conditions, effects were predominantly repulsive or near zero in both identification and discrimination. In contrast, eliminating target-specific information reversed ensemble-induced bias from repulsion to attraction. Identification precision also decreased systematically from pre-cue to post-cue to no-cue conditions. Study 2 replicated this cue-dependent pattern in graphical displays of startup valuations and precinct vote contributions. Our findings isolate attentional certainty as a key determinant of whether ensemble context repels or attracts individual-item representations, extending the design question beyond precision to how attention directing choices determine which bias the viewer will be operating under.

papers.title: Semantic Validity vs. Graphical Arrangement in Visualization Grammars
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21073v1

summary.background:
- Grammar of Graphics: Leland Wilkinson's idea that a chart can be built from separate parts (data, transformations, marks, coordinates), much like a sentence is built from grammar rules.
- Visualization grammar: a software system that lets users specify charts declaratively, by describing what they want rather than drawing each element.
- Statistical graphics vs. information visualization (InfoVis): two research communities; the first emphasizes statistical correctness, the second often emphasizes expressive design.
- Semantic validity: whether a chart's transformations and encodings are correct for the data's meaning and the statistics involved.
- Expressivity vs. validity: the more freely a user can arrange graphics, the more easily a meaningless chart can be produced.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes three contribution types (Semantic Validity Theories, Semantic Visualization Systems, and Graphical Arrangement Systems) to clarify the trade-off between enforcing statistical or data correctness and allowing graphical flexibility in Grammar of Graphics-inspired visualization tools.
summary.plain: Software tools for making charts often describe a picture in layers and parts, following a framework called the Grammar of Graphics. This paper argues that these tools differ a lot: some strictly check that a chart makes statistical sense, while others give the user free rein over how things look. The authors propose three categories to label such work so that researchers from data-visualization and statistics communities can compare and combine their efforts more easily.
summary.why: Charting software is used widely in science and business, and the choice between strict checking and creative freedom affects what users can do and how mistakes are caught. The text is a conceptual framing; it does not report measured outcomes, so its practical impact is uncertain and would depend on how the categories are adopted by the field.

papers.abstract: Systems for modular, declarative and compositional specification for data visualizations, otherwise known as visualization grammars, often claim Wilkinson's Grammar of Graphics as motivation, inspiration or foundation. However, despite the shared intellectual lineage, visualization grammars can vary greatly in design scope and focus. In particular, systems that strongly adhere to domain-specific notions of correctness must trade-off expressivity for validity. This trade-off between semantics and graphical flexibility is currently under-articulated, leading to difficulty integrating various GoG-inspired visualization contributions, especially between InfoVis and Statistical Graphics. We propose three new types of visualization contributions to support such integration: Semantic Validity Theories, Semantic Visualization Systems and Graphical Arrangement Systems. The first two prioritize the adherence of data visualizations to correctness conditions, such as statistical or mathematical transformations and data semantics, whilst the third largely leave validity concerns to the user. We illustrate these new contribution types using examples from two recent grammar of graphics inspired papers, and show how they supported more nuanced notions of expressivity and usability in evaluation and design of visualization systems.

papers.title: A Line is Not Just a Line: Visualizing Harmonious Complex Line Sets
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20190v1

summary.background:
- Visualization: turning data into images so patterns can be seen.
- 3D computer graphics: software that renders objects and scenes in three dimensions.
- Line quality: variations in a line's thickness, texture, edge, or style, which artists use to suggest form and mood.
- Portfolio paper: a collection of design examples with reflections, rather than a controlled experiment.
- Human-computer interaction: the field that studies how people design and use computer systems and images.
summary.one_liner: A portfolio of visual design studies that explores how varying the character of lines (quality, weight, and style) in 3D scientific visualizations, especially climate data, can improve clarity and add a handcrafted feel.
summary.plain: Computer pictures of science, such as 3D charts of climate data, often draw every line the same plain way, so the lines carry little meaning beyond showing a path or edge. This portfolio presents a set of design experiments and lessons learned showing how varying the look of lines, much as artists do by hand, can make such images clearer and more human. The text describes the designs and lessons but does not report measured results from user testing.
summary.why: Scientific visualizations are used to communicate issues like climate change, so clearer and more engaging pictures could matter for public understanding. The text does not show whether these designs actually improve comprehension, so its practical impact remains to be tested.

papers.abstract: Line is a foundational building block in visual design for traditional media and computer graphics. Controlled variation in line quality can be used to define form, create abstractions, distinguish categories, control affect, and more. Yet, when it comes to computer graphics visualizations of science, particularly those built upon 3D computer graphics, too often a line is just a line. This portfolio presents a series of visual design studies and lessons learned that explore the diverse character of line that might be useful for 3D visualizations. The imagery begins to show how more sophisticated use of this powerful visual building block could increase the clarity of data visualizations while also bringing a human, handcrafted aesthetic that reinforces the people and impacts behind scientific climate data.
